text: By means of the great dam, on the Blue Nile at Makwar, the opening ceremony of which was performed today by Lord Lloyd High Commissioner for the Soudan, a vast region in the Soudan is converted from a barren steppe and enhanced by a few semi-normal clans into the living agricultural country.

label: text
text: The immediate area brought into cultivation is 300,000 acres of black soil admirably suited for growing cotton. Crops are being grown on three years' rotation; soil being one year under cotton, second under "Habibia" and a third year Fallow.

label: text
text: The reservoir above the dam consists of a length of 30 miles and a maximum height of 40 metres. It is constructed of solid masonry, granite being obtained from quarries in the neighbourhood. The major portion is composed of masonry set in cement mortar with facing of Portland cement. Suice openings are lined with dressed ashlar. At the end of the masonry portions, the dam is continued on both east and west sides by an earth embankment with a heavy concrete facing wall on the upstream side.

label: text
text: In the presence of Sir Geoffrey Archer, two hundred European guests, and ten thousand natives, Lord Lloyd formally inaugurated the Makwar Danr by operating a special switch in the form of, a silver statuette of Amenhemat II, the first known irrigator of ancient Egypt, thereby opening the stulics, after which the inflowing waters were blessed by the Rt. Rev. H. L. Gwynne, D.D., Bishop of Egypt and the Soudan, and the Grand Cadir of the Soudan.

label: text
text: At the opening of the Makwar Dam Lord Lloyd paid a tribute to the genius and patience of Lord Cromer, of which the Soudan was now reaping the fruits. He emphasised that Egypt had no need to be alarmed that the new dam would deprive Egypt of water. He said that there should now be no difficulty in reaching a settlement, simply guaranteeing the needs of Egypt and simultaneously allowing the Soudan to make steady progress and development.

label: text
text: Pasha Small Sirry, the Egyptian Minister for Public Works, who was present at the ceremony, voiced pride in the part played by Egypt in initiating the Gezirs irrigation project. He had no doubt that a water supply, artificially controlled, was simply sufficient for all their demands.

text: Ignatius Emanuel Lincoln, aged 23, a Bombardier in the Royal Horse Artillery, was to-day sentenced to death at Devizes, for the murder of Edward Richard Brewers, traveller.

label: text
text: Richard was found shot in his garden at Trowbridge on Christmas Eve. Lincoln and a fellow-soldier named Ian Stewart were charged with the crime. Lincoln gave evidence how he and Stewart went to the house of Richards at night, whilst Richards was away, to try to get money, which they believed was in the house. They entered the house by an unlocked door, but obtained no money. They drank brandy and beer which they found, and were still in the house when Richards appeared at the door. Lincoln admitted that in an endeavour to escape he fired his automatic pistol several times in the direction of Richards, who cried out that he was hit.

label: text
text: The other soldier was acquitted of murder, but was re-arrested for burglary.

label: text
text: A notable feature of the case is that Lincoln is the son of Trebitch Lincoln, an alien who was at one time a member of the British Parliament and was during the war on his own confession found guilty of espionage and deported to Prague.

text: Mr. Lloyd George's speech at Carnarvon yesterday, in which he declared that the Liberal Party would not at this moment negotiate an alliance with the Labour Party but would strive to increase its own strength, is the subject of varied comment to-day.

label: text
text: Mr. Charles G. Ammon, who was a member of the late Labour Government, declared that he did not think there could ever be a coalition of Liberal and Labour, but he believed that some of the Liberals would come over to the Labour Party.

label: text
text: Commander the Hon. Joseph Kenworthy, M.P., who is one of the leading younger Liberals, declared in favour of an immediate active working arrangement between the Labour and Liberal Parties in preparation for the formation of an alternative Government. He is reported to have added: "We cannot go on with the Conservative Party in power and no strong alternative Government. If certain leaders stand in the way we will find means of getting over that."

text: A noticeable feature of recent speeches by miners' leaders is their earnest desire to prevent a strike when, in the month of May, the coal situation will come under review owing to the expiration of present subsidy.

label: text
text: Mr. A. J. Cook, Secretary of the Miners' Federation, has expressed strong hopes that an amicable settlement may be reached; and another member of the Federation, Mr. F. B. Varley, M.P., declared last night that he did not believe that a crisis was inevitable.

label: text
text: A similar view was expressed by the Rt. Hon. W. C. Bridgeman, who is one of the Members of the Cabinet, who took a leading part in the negotiations between the miners, mine owners, and the Government, when the dispute was in its more acute stage some months ago.

text: History tells us that Dick Turpin was a sordid enough rogue, but romance has painted his career in glowing colours. When his story came to be filmed there could be no doubt as to which version the cinema would take. The picture now showing at the Queen's Theatre lacks nothing of romance and high adventure. Tom Mix plays the title role and his favourite mount the part of Black Beas. Both win all hearts by their spirit and dash—especially in the famous ride from London to New York, when they outdistance the Bow Street Runners in the race to save the highwayman's beautiful lady love from the clutches of the unpleasant young lord who would marry her against her will. Dick Turpin's friend, King figures in the picture, and there are thrilling events aplenty, not the least of these being an old-style boxing match and an escape from the very noose of the hangman.

text: Mr. C. W. Barron, proprietor of the "Wall-street Journal" and other American publications, has cabled, for publication in America, a reply to Mr. George Harvey's recent article in the "North American Review," in which the late American Ambassador in London painted a gloomy picture of Great Britain's future as an industrial and commercial power.

label: text
text: Mr. Barron, after referring to the British arguments used in the conversations with Mr. Harvey before the debt settlement, writes:

label: text
text: Evidently the arguments against which Mr. Harvey combated I have had a strong after-effect upon his mental vision. But Mr. Harvey should have delved deeper into British finance. You cannot safely take the Englishman at his own depreciated valuation.

label: text
text: The following are among the salient passages in Mr. Barron's statement:

label: text
text: The main contention of Mr. Harvey would be laughable if the discussion of it were not in danger of taking on a serious international aspect. Before writing the doom of Great Britain, burdened by a mountain of debt, Mr. Harvey should have had a clearer solution for this problem: How can a man go broke by writing his own notes, payable only to himself?

label: text
text: The way most the three big successful Powers each forty billion dollars and more later. The United States and Great Britain laid on the taxes and have to date paid a large part of the cost—the United States nearly one-half and Great Britain several billions. France looked to Germany to pay and now must suffer, to use the language of her new Finance Minister, "taxes infernal". BUT BRITAIN PAYS IT ALL.

label: text
text: Great Britain pays, three hundred million pounds, or a billion and a half dollars, to her own subjects as interest on her war bonds, and a good measure of this she takes back in taxes. But her total debt service is not one-half her government expenditure. She has a budget of eight hundred million pounds, or nearly four billion dollars. This is much greater than that of the United States.

label: text
text: But she collects it all, and if she has a deficit this year it will be only because she has elected to pay twenty million pounds, or a hundred million dollars, to subsidise her coal interests while she takes time to solve the problem of her fuel supply and throw the Bolsheviks out of the country.

label: text
text: England was the great, war sufferer. She had most to lose in trade, shipping, coal, and manufacturing. But in seven years after the war, she has balanced her budget, advanced the pound sterling by fifty per cent. to its parity with the U.S. gold dollar, settled Ireland, and thrown over free trade.

text: There are many factors in English progress. Chief among them are capital, labour, confidence, and security, with wise administration.
